themes.theme: Provider and deployer roles, and when they shift
themes.definition: Rules that decide which organisation carries the AI Act's provider or deployer obligations for a system, including when a public body, a deployer or another third party becomes the provider.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act makes one 'natural or legal person, defined as the provider' take responsibility for placing a high-risk system on the market or into service, whether or not it designed the system, and an operator that holds several roles must meet all their obligations cumulatively (Recitals 79 and 83). A distributor, importer, deployer or other third party becomes the provider, with all Article 16 duties, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk system, makes a substantial modification, or changes a system's intended purpose (Recital 84, Art. 25(1)); the Omnibus makes the value-chain duties in Art. 25(2) and (4) fineable, and EU088 says a downstream modifier of a systemic-risk model must notify the Commission as a provider. The Commission's guidelines on prohibitions (EU043) and on Article 50 (EU_Art50) apply this to public bodies: a public authority that builds a system or chatbot in-house for its own use is both provider and deployer; the organisation stays the deployer when contractors or freelancers operate the system for it; its individual employees are not deployers; and staff using AI at work fall under the organisation's transparency duties. EU043 adds that a deployer answers for a prohibited use even if the provider's terms of use excluded that use. The JRC handbook (JRC129100) treats responsibility along the chain as unsettled: it calls for every actor to have 'identifiable responsibilities' and asks, as an open question, how far procured solution providers 'can be held accountable'. [inference] Across these documents accountability attaches to organisations, not to named officials.
themes.holders: Providers; deployers; distributors, importers and other third parties who rebrand, substantially modify or repurpose a system; public authorities that develop systems in-house; legal persons that use contractors or freelancers; downstream modifiers of general-purpose AI models; 'each actor operating in the ecosystem' (JRC129100).
themes.binding: Art. 25(1) is statutory ('shall be considered'); a party that becomes the provider is fineable for breach of the Art. 16 provider duties up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% (Art. 99(4)(a)), and the Omnibus adds Art. 25(2) and (4) to the fineable list (Art. 99(4)(da)). The recitals and the Commission guidelines are non-binding interpretation; the JRC passages are recommendations and open questions with no consequence.

themes.theme: Authorised representatives and identifiable contact points
themes.definition: Requirements that a provider outside the EU appoint a representative in the Union whom authorities can address, and that providers be identifiable and contactable.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers established outside the EU must, before making a high-risk system available (Art. 22) or placing a general-purpose AI model on the market (Art. 54; EU088 para 48), appoint by written mandate an authorised representative established in the Union. The mandate must let competent authorities, and for models the AI Office, address the representative 'in addition to or instead of the provider' on all compliance issues; the representative keeps the declaration, technical documentation and certificate for ten years and supplies them on reasoned request. The representative must end the mandate if it has reason to think the provider is breaking its obligations, and must then immediately inform the market surveillance authority (or, for models, the AI Office) and give its reasons, so the representative also works as a check on its own principal. Testing in real-world conditions likewise requires a provider established in the Union or a legal representative there (Art. 60(4)(d)), and every high-risk system must carry the provider's name and a contact address on the system, its packaging or its documentation (Art. 16(b)). [inference] For a public body buying from a non-EU supplier this gives regulators a party in the Union to address, but no passage says the public body itself can call on the representative.
themes.holders: Providers established in third countries (of high-risk systems and of general-purpose AI models); authorised representatives; providers and prospective providers testing in real-world conditions; providers of high-risk systems (name and contact).
themes.binding: Statutory duties in the Articles ('shall'); Recital 82 uses 'should'. Having no authorised representative is formal non-compliance (Art. 83(1)), and representatives' duties are fineable under Art. 99(4)(b); for model providers, fines under Art. 101; testing may not proceed without a Union-based provider or representative (Art. 60(4)). EU088 restates the statutory duty.

quotes.quote: Prior to making their high-risk AI systems available on the Union market, providers established in third countries shall, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative which is established in the Union.

The mandate shall empower the authorised representative to be addressed, in addition to or instead of the provider, by the competent authorities, on all issues related to ensuring compliance with this Regulation.
The authorised representative shall terminate the mandate if it considers or has reason to consider the provider to be acting contrary to its obligations pursuant to this Regulation.
providers established or located within a third country must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union before placing a general-purpose AI model on the Union market

themes.theme: Controller responsibility under data protection law
themes.definition: Allocation, under the EU data protection regulations, of the accountable 'controller' role for AI processing to the organisation that decides why and how the processing happens, with the duty to demonstrate compliance that goes with it.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPS orientations on generative AI, the EDPS risk guidance and the EDPB Opinion (EU074) place accountability for AI processing on the controller: the organisation that decides to develop an AI system, use a service provider for development, or deploy a generative system for a purpose. If an EU institution outsources model development it 'remains a controller' and the vendor is a processor; third parties that build datasets on their own account are controllers of that processing; and roles should be assessed case by case before processing starts (EU074 para 62) and written into the records of processing. Controllers 'shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with' the data protection principles (EU074), responsibility stays with the controller rather than the data protection officer, and EU institutions are accountable for transfers made on their behalf, including by cloud processors, inside and outside the EEA. Controllers 'remain fully responsible' for their own compliance assessments even when they use the EDPS risk framework, and EU institutions must identify and mitigate risks to rights 'and to demonstrate how they did so' (EDPS_AI_risk). The principle of accountability requires responsibilities to be 'clearly identified and respected' along the generative AI supply chain. To whom the controller answers is mostly not stated in these passages [inference: the EDPS for EU institutions, national supervisory authorities otherwise].
themes.holders: Controllers, in particular EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies (EUIs); processors, including AI developers working on an EUI's behalf; third parties that create training datasets on their own account; all actors in the generative AI supply chain.
themes.binding: Restatements of statutory duties under the EUDPR and GDPR (accountability principle, Art. 5(2) GDPR and its EUDPR equivalent) inside non-binding guidance; some steps are recommendations ('should conduct a thorough assessment'). Consequences are not stated in these passages; the supervisory consequences appear in the theme on data protection supervisors.

quotes.quote: an entity that determines “why” and “how” processing takes place includes an organization that decides to develop an AI system, use a service provider for development, and/ or deploy a generative system for a specific purpose.

themes.theme: Responsibility that stays put when AI outputs, suppliers or staff are involved
themes.definition: Statements that relying on an AI output, a supplier, a third-party tool or a contractor does not move responsibility away from the public body, provider or staff member that uses it.
themes.what_is_set_out: Several documents insist that responsibility does not move to the tool, the supplier or the AI output. The AI Act (Recital 22, restated by EU043) says national authorities and Union bodies that use outputs of AI systems run by excluded third-country authorities or international organisations 'remain accountable' for complying with Union law, and EU043 says deployers 'remain responsible' for ensuring employees are not adversely affected by AI used on them and answer for prohibited uses whatever the supplier's contract says. Providers that rely on upstream or third-party marking solutions keep their own responsibility for marking outputs (EU_Art50 para 74; EU121 Measure 1.1), an EU institution that outsources model development stays the controller, and responsibility stays with the controller rather than the data protection officer. The EDPS splits responsibility for personal data in outputs by origin: the provider is responsible if the output stems from the original training data, while the user of the system may be responsible where it derives from statistical inferences (fn 52; the input note is cut off before saying on what data). The European Court of Auditors applies the principle to its own use: AI may support financial operations and HR compliance checks only with controls and 'human oversight', and 'final responsibility' and 'accountability for control results' remain with staff. None of these passages says to whom the responsibility is owed or what follows if it is not met, beyond the AI Act fines attached to the underlying duties.
themes.holders: Recipient national authorities and Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies using AI outputs; deployers (including employers); providers of generative AI systems and code Signatories; controllers and EUIs; ECA staff; providers and users of generative AI systems (for outputs containing personal data).
themes.binding: Recital 22 and its restatement are non-binding; EU043 and EU_Art50 are non-binding interpretations of statutory duties (Art. 50 breaches are fineable); EU121 is a code commitment for Signatories; the EDPS passages are non-binding interpretation; the ECA passages are internal conditions on its own use. No consequence is stated for the retained responsibility itself.
themes.checks: ECA (Action 9): trigger: any AI-assisted financial operation or routine compliance check; compared against: not stated; metric or threshold: not stated ('controls are in place to provide accuracy' is named without a measure); who: staff, under human oversight; what happens with the result: staff carry final responsibility and accountability for control results. Other passages: n/a.

quotes.quote: Recipient national authorities and Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies making use of such outputs in the Union remain accountable to ensure their use complies with Union law.

themes.theme: Internal accountability lines inside EU institutions and providers
themes.definition: Reporting lines, oversight bodies and internal frameworks through which those running AI inside an organisation answer to its own boards or leadership.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission's AI@EC communication sets an internal reporting chain: the Interservice Steering Group on AI reports 'on a regular basis' to the IT and Cybersecurity Board (ITCB) and the IMSB and channels projects to corporate IT governance, the ITCB 'will regularly report major AI projects' to the Corporate Management Board, and the Member(s) of the Commission in charge of digital transformation, HR and administration oversee implementation and report to the College. The European Parliament's 2024 framework (proposed, awaiting Bureau approval) says the governance framework shall ensure consistent treatment of AI initiatives 'with clear accountability and transparency', asks the Governance Board Chair to send regular roadmap updates to the Bureau's Working Group on ICT, and says non-compliance with the assessment process 'should lead to the suspension of the AI project'. The ECA says the move to corporate AI agents 'will require updated governance, clear accountability, and new controls' without allocating them, and the JRC's 2025 report suggests 'clearly establishing roles and responsibilities, creating oversight mechanisms'. For providers, the AI Act's quality management system must include 'an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of the management and other staff' (Art. 17(1)(m)). Frequencies ('regular'), thresholds ('major') and consequences are undefined; the only consequence stated is the Parliament's suspension, and who suspends is not stated.
themes.holders: Interservice Steering Group on AI (ISG-AI); ITCB; Member(s) of the Commission in charge of digital transformation, human resources and administration; EP Governance Board Chair; ECA; public administrations (JRC, unnamed); providers' management and staff.
themes.binding: Internal Commission mandates (AIatEC); a proposed internal framework using 'shall' and 'should' (EP2024); an institutional principle (ECA, 'will require'); a suggestion (JRC, 'may entail'); a statutory duty for providers' quality management systems (Art. 17, fineable through Art. 16(c) and Art. 99(4)(a)). No consequence is stated for failing to report.
themes.checks: EP2024 suspension: trigger: non-compliance with the risk and impact assessment process; compared against: the assessment process; metric or threshold: not stated; who: not stated; what happens with the result: suspension of the AI project. Other passages: n/a.

themes.theme: Sign-off: declarations of conformity, CE marking and signed records
themes.definition: Formal acts by which a named person or organisation puts its name to a system's compliance, such as a signed declaration, a conformity mark or signed test reports.
themes.what_is_set_out: Under the AI Act the provider draws up an EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk system and, by doing so, 'shall assume responsibility' for meeting the Section 2 requirements (Art. 47(4)); the declaration states that it is issued 'under the sole responsibility of the provider' and carries the name, function and signature of the person who signed it (Annex V). The CE marking must be affixed 'visibly, legibly and indelibly', with a digital marking for systems provided only digitally (Art. 48(3), Recital 129). The technical documentation must include 'test logs and all test reports dated and signed by the responsible persons' (Annex IV 2(g)), although to whom those signers answer is not stated. Outside the AI Act, the EDPS asks EU institutions to document 'the final assessment that the generative AI is trustworthy' [inference: this works as an internal sign-off, but no signatory, recipient or effect on use is stated], and the JRC handbook suggests sustainability certification and labelling as a public signal of compliance. No passage requires a public body, as deployer, to sign off a tool before using it; formal sign-off falls on providers.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk AI systems; the person who signs the declaration for the provider; the provider's 'responsible persons' for testing; EUIs (EDPS); unnamed actors (JRC).
themes.binding: AI Act statutory duties; a missing or incorrect declaration or CE marking is formal non-compliance under Art. 83(1), on which the market surveillance authority requires the provider to end the non-compliance and may then restrict or prohibit the system. The EDPS step is a recommendation; the JRC item is a suggestion ('This could be done by').
themes.checks: Signed test logs (Annex IV 2(g)): trigger: testing during development, before the system is placed on the market [inference]; compared against: not stated in the passage; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the provider's responsible persons sign; what happens with the result: kept in the technical documentation available to supervisors. Declaration of conformity: trigger: before placing on the market; compared against: the Section 2 requirements; metric: not stated; who: the provider; result: the provider assumes responsibility.

themes.theme: Burden on operators to demonstrate compliance, lawfulness or an exception
themes.definition: Provisions that place the burden of proof on the provider, deployer or institution to show that a practice is legitimate, an exception applies or processing is lawful.
themes.what_is_set_out: Several documents put the burden of proof on the operator rather than on the supervisor. EU043 says that in checks by market surveillance authorities 'it is on the provider and the deployer ... to demonstrate that the AI practice is legitimate and justified', and EU_Art50 says providers who rely on an exception to the duty to disclose AI interaction 'will need to assess and demonstrate' that it applies. For EU institutions, the EDPS says they must identify and mitigate risks 'and to demonstrate how they did so', carry 'a specific responsibility' to demonstrate lawfulness, including for a model developed by others, must justify why web scraping is necessary for tasks prescribed by EU law, and should be able to show they can rely on an Article 24(2) exception before using automated decisions such as CV screening. To whom the demonstration is owed is usually not stated [inference: the market surveillance authority or the EDPS].
themes.holders: Providers and deployers of AI systems (each within their responsibilities); providers relying on transparency exceptions; EUIs as controllers.
themes.binding: Non-binding interpretation (Commission guidelines, EDPS guidance) of statutory duties. Where the demonstration fails, the exception is lost and the duty applies (EU_Art50, with fines under Art. 99(4)(g)); under EU043 the practice may fall within a prohibition [inference]; otherwise consequences are not stated.
themes.checks: MSA checks (EU043): trigger: not stated; compared against: whether the practice is 'legitimate and justified'; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the provider and deployer must demonstrate and the market surveillance authority checks; what happens with the result: not stated. EDPS duties: trigger: before processing or before relying on an exception; compared against: EUDPR lawfulness conditions and Art. 24(2) exceptions; metric: not stated; who: the EUI; result: not stated.

themes.theme: Codes of practice, standards and comply-or-explain
themes.definition: Routes by which providers and deployers can show compliance by adhering to an approved code of practice or standard, and the extra scrutiny that falls on those who do not.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act lets providers of high-risk systems or general-purpose models that do not follow common specifications 'duly justify' technical solutions of at least equivalent level (Art. 41(5), with the recipient of the justification not stated), and requires model providers who do not follow an approved code of practice or harmonised standard to 'demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission' (Art. 53(4), 55(2)). The Commission's guidelines (EU088, EU_Art50) turn this into two tracks: signatories of a code assessed as adequate are supervised mainly on whether they adhered, gain 'increased trust', and may have their commitments counted as a mitigating factor when fines are set; non-signatories are 'expected to demonstrate' compliance by other means, report their measures to the AI Office and may face more requests for information. The transparency code (EU121) uses 'will' for measures that are mandatory for signatories and 'monitored by competent market surveillance authorities', lets providers demonstrate compliance through 'documented internal testing' subject to authority review, and says sectoral good practices under the code will be published. Code participants report regularly to the AI Office, including against key performance indicators, and the AI Office and Board publish their assessment of the codes' adequacy, a task the Omnibus gives to the Commission alone. EU088 adds that the AI Office may take account of technical standards when assessing providers' cybersecurity, accountability and governance processes.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk AI systems and of general-purpose AI models; providers and deployers within Art. 50(2) and (4); code Signatories; participants in codes of practice; AI Office, Board and Commission (assessors); competent market surveillance authorities.
themes.binding: Statutory comply-or-explain in the AI Act ('shall duly justify', 'shall demonstrate'); adherence to codes is voluntary, but measures marked 'will' are mandatory for Signatories; the Commission guidelines are non-binding. Stated consequences: loss of the benefit of facilitated compliance on opting out, more requests for information for non-signatories, and code adherence as a possible mitigating factor in fines.
themes.checks: EU121 Measure 1.1: trigger: not stated (demonstration of compliance for marking); compared against: the requirements in Commitment 3; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the Signatory tests internally and documents it, competent market surveillance authorities review; what happens with the result: subject to authority review. Codes of practice (Art. 56): participants report on implementation, measures and outcomes, including against key performance indicators; the AI Office and Board monitor and publish their assessment.
